name: Jamal Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, thanks for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. All right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I'm home this week, so I've got time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm fly-in fly-out, which means I fly to the mine and live in the camp for two weeks, then fly home for one. I drive a loader underground at a gold mine, a low, long machine we call a bogger that scoops broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass. It's hot, dark, and you're always watching the walls and the ventilation. I'm still learning to tram, which is driving in tight tunnels, without scraping the walls, and my supervisor, Ahmed, writes it up every time I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use a chatbot now and then to write emails, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say in the crib room, our lunch area underground, that it was overhyped like most things. Online I'd maybe share a joke meme about it, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays, which is good, but the life is still hard. Two weeks underground and one week home is hard on a couple, AI or no AI. We're saving for a wedding and a house deposit, and FIFO pay is the only way we'll get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my swings, which is what we call a two-week stint, and get signed off on the bigger loader by next winter. We'd keep putting most of my overtime into the house fund, we're at about four months of savings plus the wedding pot. And I'd keep using the chatbot for small stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit uneasy because the FIFO life isn't something I want forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia works at a bank call centre in the city, answering customers about cards and loans. She hates the targets, but it's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the plateau picture that touches Sofia's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. The bank already has a chatbot on the website, and it takes some of the easy calls. If it stays like that, she's fine.

say: AI was **overhyped**, like most things people talk about in the crib room.
He'd share a **joke meme** online, nothing serious.
think: His job **stays**, but fly-in fly-out life is still hard.
They need **FIFO pay** for the wedding and house deposit.
do: Get signed off on the **bigger loader** by next winter.
Put most **overtime** into the house fund.
feel: Mostly **fine**, slightly uneasy about the long-term toll of FIFO.
S0.quote: Two weeks underground and one week home is hard on a couple, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: His pressure is **relationship strain** and saving, not technology.
Partner's **call centre** job already feels a small chatbot effect.
He calls the job steady but clearly doesn't want **FIFO forever**.

steps.text: Get signed off on the bigger underground loader by next winter
Put most overtime into the house deposit fund
Keep using a chatbot to write work emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers, that's Sofia. That's the first thing I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office jobs are in trouble and the underground jobs are fine for now. I'd say it carefully, because half the camp has partners in office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be okay on my wage, but only just. My partner answers phones at a bank call centre, so in this picture the risky job in our house isn't mine. Some underground mines already run loaders by remote control from the surface, so my job isn't safe forever either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Sofia look at moving into something less exposed, maybe a bank branch role or a course in bookkeeping, though even that is thinking work. We'd push the wedding back a year and save harder. I'd ask Ahmed about the remote loader training, since I'd rather drive from a chair on the surface than lose the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, mostly for her. And a bit guilty I'm away two weeks when she's going through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're a team and my pay can carry us for a while. Then I'd probably ask too many questions about her targets and annoy her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own job isn't safe forever. When does that bite?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they bring remote loaders here, maybe three or four years. I'd want to be one of the people they train, not one of the ones they let go.

say: **Office jobs** are in trouble; underground is fine for now.
He'd say it **carefully**, since many camp partners work in offices.
think: His partner's **call centre** job is the household's main risk.
**Remote loaders** mean his own job isn't safe forever.
do: Help his partner look at **less exposed** work or a bookkeeping course.
Push the **wedding** back a year and save harder.
feel: **Worried** for his partner and **guilty** about being away two weeks at a time.
S1.quote: My partner answers phones at a bank call centre, so in this picture the risky job in our house isn't mine.
fieldNote: The household's exposure runs through his partner's **call centre** job.
He knows **remote-controlled loaders** exist and wants to be trained, not cut.
The **wedding delay** is the first concrete cost of this picture.

steps.text: Push the wedding back a year and save harder
Help Sofia apply for a bank branch role or bookkeeping course
Ask Ahmed for a spot on the remote loader training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's when we were getting married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to slow it down or pay people while they adjust. I'm not a big politics guy, but you'd need something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Sofia loses her job in 2028 and I lose mine around 2031. We'd planned the wedding for 2028, and I can't see us spending wedding money while both our jobs are on a timer. That's the first thing that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the wedding venue and keep the deposit money as savings. I'd look at getting a trade ticket fast, maybe a gas fitter, while I'm still earning FIFO money. We'd probably move in with my parents to save rent if Sofia's job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Both of us at once is the bit I can't get past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need the spare room for a while. My dad would say yes before I finished asking, but I'd feel like I was nineteen again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With the robots three years later, what's the plan for your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeeze every swing I can, all the overtime. Every swing between 2028 and 2031 is money in the bank while Sofia finds something.

say: Governments need to **slow it down** or pay people while they adjust.
He's not political, but says **something** would be needed.
think: His partner loses her job in **2028**, and he loses his around **2031**.
The **wedding money** can't be spent while both jobs are on a timer.
do: Cancel the **wedding venue** and keep the deposit as savings.
Get a **trade ticket**, maybe gas fitting, while earning FIFO money.
Move in with his **parents** to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed** that both household jobs go at once.
S2.quote: We'd planned the wedding for 2028, and I can't see us spending wedding money while both our jobs are on a timer.
fieldNote: He clearly sees the **three-year gap**: his partner first, then his own job.
Every **FIFO swing** becomes savings time before the robots arrive.
Moving in with his parents feels like **going backwards** to him.

steps.text: Cancel the wedding venue and bank the deposit
Start a gas fitter trade ticket while still on FIFO pay
Move into his parents' spare room to save rent
Work every overtime swing between 2028 and 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then robots around 2034. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, but we've got time to prepare if the companies are honest about it. I'd tell the boys in camp to start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd move Sofia first, because her job goes first. Five years is enough to change one of our jobs, but probably not both at once. So she retrains, I keep earning, and then we swap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia would start a two-year course in something hands-on, maybe dental assisting, next year while I cover the bills. We'd still get married, but small, at the community hall, in 2028. Once she's working, I'd start a trade around 2030, before the robots come for the loaders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's like doing two shifts in a row, you know it's tiring but you know when it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first to pay for her course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My car. I'd sell the ute and use the camp bus and her little hatchback. It's a few hundred a month we don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it matter to you which of you studies first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My dad would say the man should carry it, but that's his generation. Whoever's job goes first studies first.

He'd tell his mates in camp to **start thinking** now.
think: His partner's job goes first, so she should **retrain first**.
Five years allows **one switch**, then they swap roles.
do: Pay the bills while his partner does a **dental assisting** course.
Hold a **small wedding** at the community hall in 2028.
Start a **trade** around 2030, before robots reach loaders.
feel: **Anxious** but steadied by a clear plan.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to change one of our jobs, but probably not both at once.
fieldNote: He builds a **turn-taking plan**: partner retrains first, then him.
The **wedding** survives, downsized, rather than being cancelled.
He sets aside his father's view on **gender roles** for practical reasons.

steps.text: Pay the bills while Sofia studies dental assisting
Start a trade course around 2030 before robots reach loaders
Sell the ute and ride the camp bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI arrives, nearly forty for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway, and anyone sensible should use it. I'd probably share some articles in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's manageable. Give me ten years and I'll have a trade, a small house and a wife who isn't stuck on hold. Sofia would have time to leave the call centre on her own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing FIFO for maybe four more years to build the house deposit. Sofia would study part-time while working. Around 2030 I'd start an electrical apprenticeship and come home for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. More like planning a long drive than running from a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you start a family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After I'm off FIFO. I don't want to be the dad who's underground for half the kid's birthdays. So maybe 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house price, probably. If everyone in the city loses office jobs, who knows what happens to prices. That I can't plan for.

say: It's a **long runway**, and sensible people should use it.
He'd share **articles** in the family group chat.
think: Ten years is **manageable** for both of them.
His partner could leave the call centre **on her own terms**.
do: Do **four more years** of FIFO for the house deposit.
Start an **electrical apprenticeship** around 2030 and come home.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, like planning a long drive.
S4.quote: Give me ten years and I'll have a trade, a small house and a wife who isn't stuck on hold.
fieldNote: With ten years both jobs look safe for **the next few years**, so worry eases.
**Children** wait until he leaves FIFO, around 2031.
His remaining doubt is **house prices**, which he admits he can't predict.

steps.text: Do four more years of FIFO to build the house deposit
Plan a first child for after leaving FIFO

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes both our jobs within three years. Underground you learn to listen for the rock moving before it falls, and this AI stuff is the rock moving. What would help is retraining you can do on rotation, like online courses that fit swings, and some income support for people like Sofia.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the camp. Hundreds of us live there. If the loaders run themselves, the camp cooks and cleaners go too, and nobody counts them.

headlineQuote: Underground you learn to listen for the rock moving before it falls, and this AI stuff is the rock moving.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old underground loader** operator at a gold mine, working fly-in fly-out.
He's saving for a **wedding and house** with his partner Sofia, who works at a bank call centre.
He's **pragmatic**, uses chatbots now and then, and isn't strongly political.
In every AI picture the household risk starts with **his partner's job**, then reaches his.
His plans are **turn-taking**: one retrains while the other earns.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household jobs go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Online retraining** that fits fly-in fly-out rotations.
**Income support** for call centre workers like his partner.
